title: Spectral cutoff and finite-rank source lemmas
subtitle: G2 lecture 128000 · baseline companion · needs expansion
adaptation: First-pass source-derived outline. Section excerpts and any vector equation come from the spoken lecture and its display-only mathematics appendix. Expand with worked mathematics, proofs and topic-specific diagrams.

slides.title: The problem and its setting
slides.lead: Some proofs in perturbation theory look like finite matrix arguments even when the theorem concerns an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space.
body: The missing work is often hidden in a phrase such as, pass to finite-rank cutoffs. Davis and Kahan's source includes results that justify these passages. We will study two of them: convergence of singular-value data under finite-dimensional approximation, and Lemma six point three, which says that almost saturating a leading singular-value energy budget forces an unwanted block to be small. These are analytic proof obligations.

slides.title: How a basis cutoff works
slides.lead: Choose an orthonormal basis of a Hilbert space.
body: For each finite set of basis indices, take the orthogonal projection onto their span. As the finite set grows, its projection converges strongly to the identity. Strong convergence means that for each fixed vector x, the length of the omitted tail tends to zero. It does not mean the operator norm of the difference from the identity tends to zero. If the Hilbert space is infinite dimensional, every finite-rank projection leaves some unit vector untouched in its orthogonal complement. On that vector, identity minus the projection still has norm one. This distinction prevents us from invoking operator-norm continuity without proof.

slides.title: Approximation numbers as finite-rank measurements
slides.lead: For a bounded operator T, its approximation number at index n is the infimum of the operator norm error over approximants of rank at most n, using zero-based indexing.
body: In finite dimensions these are the usual singular values in descending order. In Hilbert space they provide a useful extension even when T is not compact. Compose T on the right with an increasing finite-basis projection. The resulting operator has finite rank. Each fixed approximation singular value of these cutoffs converges to the corresponding approximation singular value of T. The proof depends on a min–max characterization, not on an invalid assertion of operator-norm convergence of the finite sections.

slides.title: Compactness gives a stronger statement
slides.lead: If T is compact, strong convergence of finite-rank projections applied on the output side upgrades to operator-norm convergence for T.
body: The reason is that T maps the unit ball to a set with compact closure, and strong convergence is uniform on compact sets. With input cutoffs, apply the same argument to the adjoint of T. In a Hilbert space the adjoint of a compact operator is compact, so both sides can be controlled. For an arbitrary bounded noncompact T, this upgrade is false. A cutoff of the identity on an infinite-dimensional space remains at operator-norm distance one from the identity, no matter how many basis vectors we include.

slides.title: Recover the square energy
slides.lead: The Hilbert–Schmidt energy is the sum of the squares of all approximation singular values, interpreted in the extended nonnegative reals when necessary.
body: For a finite-rank cutoff this is a finite sum and equals the sum of squared lengths of the operator applied to a suitable finite orthonormal basis. As the cutoffs increase, the supremum of their energies equals the full operator energy. Why is the supremum legitimate? The projection cutoffs give no larger energy than the full operator. Conversely, every finite set of coordinate contributions is eventually included, and the basis-energy identity shows that no contribution is permanently missed.

slides.title: State the finite-rank leakage problem
slides.lead: Now take a bounded operator K between two Hilbert spaces.
body: Let P be an orthogonal projection on the source and Q a projection on the target. Assume Q has rank at most a positive integer n. The key block-invariance hypothesis is that K maps vectors in the range of P into the range of Q. In operator form, K P equals Q K P. This is weaker than the tempting condition K P equals Q K. The latter would also force K to have no leakage from P perpendicular into Q, making the intended conclusion trivial. The paper assumes only the former. We want to bound the leakage operator that first restricts to P perpendicular, applies K, and then projects into Q. It is Q K times one minus P.

slides.title: What is nearly maximal singular-value energy?
slides.lead: For any operator T, take the sum of squares of its first n approximation singular values.
body: Call this its leading n energy. Suppose the leading n energy of K P is greater than the leading n energy of K minus eta squared, where eta is positive. In words, the selected source block almost captures all the leading n energy available in K. Lemma six point three says that the leakage from P perpendicular into Q has operator norm less than eta. This is an implication with a numerical deficit. It is not a statement that a large singular value alone forces a small cross block. We need near-saturation of the entire leading n square-energy budget.

slides.title: Derive the leakage inequality
slides.lead: Form L equal to Q K.
body: Since its range lies in Q, L has rank at most n. Split the source into the orthogonal pieces P and P perpendicular. The Hilbert–Schmidt square energy of L splits exactly into the square energy of L P plus that of L times one minus P. The block-invariance hypothesis identifies L P with K P. Therefore the energy of L is the energy of K P plus the energy of the leakage operator. Left compression by Q cannot increase any approximation singular value. Hence the leading n energy of L is at most that of K. Since L has rank at most n, its total Hilbert–Schmidt energy is already its leading n energy. Subtract the near-saturation inequality.

slides.title: A two-by-two witness
slides.lead: Take P and Q both as projection onto the first coordinate axis.
body: Let K have first row three and b, and second row zero and zero. Then K P maps the first axis into Q, so block invariance holds. Its leading one energy is nine. The full K has one nonzero singular value equal to the square root of nine plus b squared, so its leading one energy is nine plus b squared. The leakage Q K times one minus P has operator norm equal to the absolute value of b. The near-saturation hypothesis requires nine greater than nine plus b squared minus eta squared, equivalently b squared less than eta squared. The conclusion is exactly the same strict inequality on the leakage.

slides.title: Where the lemma enters the source
slides.lead: A finite-rank spectral selection argument may control how much of an operator's leading singular-value energy is captured by a chosen subspace.
body: Lemma six point three converts that energy information into an operator-norm bound on the unwanted cross block. The Hilbert-Schmidt Pythagorean identity can be proved in complex Hilbert space, and its real version follows by complexification with preservation of the squared norm. Other ideal norms need their own dominance argument. For unbounded operators, finite spectral cutoffs also enforce domain legality. One first proves identities on bounded spectral pieces and then passes to a limit in the topology justified by the hypotheses.

slides.title: Close
slides.lead: We now have two distinct ways to pass from infinite Hilbert-space data to finite calculations: fixed-index approximation singular values under strong basis cutoffs, and quantitative control of unwanted finite-rank blocks from near-maximal square energy.
body: The conclusion depends on the topology and norm used: strong basis cutoffs preserve fixed-vector information, whereas a square-energy saturation argument controls an unwanted block quantitatively. Neither fact licenses unrestricted operator-norm passage to a limit.
